why: Two implementations enforce `middleware.builtin.rate`, and until this table
existed nothing held them to one answer. The native host is
`RateLimitLayer` in crates/ruvyxa_middleware/src/builtin.rs, serving `ruvyxa
dev` and `ruvyxa start`. The deployed host is `rateLimitKey` and
`consumeFixedWindow` in packages/ruvyxa/runtime/serverless-handler.mjs,
serving every build any adapter emits.
They carried the same defect, and it was fixed in one of them first. At map
capacity both swept only buckets whose *whole* window had elapsed -- so
inside one window the map could not shrink at all -- and then refused every
key the map had not already seen. One client sending a distinct
`X-Api-Key` per request reaches that state on purpose, and from then until
the window rolls every new visitor gets a 429. The key was also taken
verbatim from a caller-written header with no length bound, so ten thousand
tracked keys retained tens of megabytes: the crate's `bounded memory`
promise was true of the count and not of the size.
The shared decision this table pins is two rules. Bound the key before it
is tracked, so a tracked bucket costs a fixed amount whatever the caller
wrote. And at capacity evict the least recently started bucket rather than
refusing: `fail closed` is the right answer when a limiter cannot answer,
and this one can -- it is not out of answers, it is out of slots, and a
slot can be taken back. The evicted client is re-admitted with a full
allowance the moment it returns, so a flood costs the strictness of the
limit rather than the availability of the service.
How the key is bounded is host-local and deliberately not pinned here. The
native host hashes with blake3, a workspace dependency it already links.
The deployed host cannot: serverless-handler.mjs is copied verbatim into
edge bundles, `node:crypto` is unavailable there, and `crypto.subtle` is
async while this limiter is not. It keeps an identity that is already
within the bound and truncates a longer one onto a hash of the whole. What
both must agree on is the observable contract, which is what `keyCases`
asserts: the tracked key is at most `maxKeyLength`, one identity always
produces one key, and two identities that must stay apart never collapse
into one -- because two clients sharing a bucket means either can limit the
other.
`keyCases` covers which identity the key is derived from, not how it is
spelled. `client` is the address the host attributes to the request when
the configured header cannot identify it; each replay supplies that in its
own way, because the native host reads a transport peer and a deployed
function has none. `client: null` means nothing identified the caller,
which both hosts spell `unknown`.
A value written as { repeat, times, suffix } is that string repeated that
many times with the suffix appended, so a 16 KB header value does not have
to be spelled out in this file.
`admissionCases` drives the limiter directly with keys that are already
bounded, so the map policy is tested apart from the key policy. `capacity`
means MAX_TRACKED_RATE_LIMIT_KEYS, which neither replay may hardcode. A
`staggered` prefill gives every seeded bucket a distinct start time so that
`the least recently started bucket` names exactly one of them: the two
hosts break a tie differently -- a BTreeMap answers in key order and a Map
in insertion order -- and a tie is not part of this contract.
A third replay was added with the fifth limiter in the workspace: the
`webVitals` beacon collector, whose copy of this algorithm is
`consumeFixedWindow` in packages/ruvyxa/src/plugins/shared.ts. It does not
enforce `middleware.builtin.rate` and takes its identity from a resolver
the project supplies rather than from a forwarded chain, so it replays
`admissionCases` -- the map policy, which is the shared part -- and only
the *bound* from `keyCases`, not which header an identity is derived from.
Retry-After is deliberately absent. The native host truncates the
remaining window to whole seconds and the deployed host rounds it up, so
they differ by one second on the same bucket. That divergence is real but
it is not this contract, and encoding it here would freeze it.

keyCases.name: a configured header is the identity
an absent key header falls back to the client, not one shared bucket
an empty key header is as absent as a missing one
no header and no attributable client is unattributable
ip keying tracks the attributed client
a 16 KB header value is bounded before it is tracked

admissionCases.name: an ordinary client spends its allowance and is then refused
a full map of expired buckets is swept rather than evicted
a full map of unexpired buckets still admits a brand new client
admitting a new client costs one bucket, not the whole allowance

$comment: Whether a CORS preflight spends a token, and what a refusal owes.
It spends one. The native host puts the limiter outside CORS on purpose
so an `OPTIONS` is charged like anything else; the deployed handler
answered preflights first and charged nothing. The same `rateLimit.max`
then bought a different number of real requests depending on where a
project was deployed, and a cross-origin page sends one preflight for
`allowOrigin` and the negotiation headers are separate questions. A 429
owes the browser `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, or the page sees an
opaque network failure instead of a rate limit. It does *not* owe
`Access-Control-Allow-Methods`: a refusal is not a preflight answer, and
sending the negotiation set would claim the request was approved.

cases.name: a preflight spends a token like any other request
a refused preflight still names the origin it refused
an ordinary cross-origin request is charged the same way
